𝐌𝐀𝐑𝐆𝐈𝐍 𝐂𝐀𝐋𝐋, 𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟏.⁣
⁣
This is maybe one of the most underrated financial movies of all time. 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥 (𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟏) takes place over roughly 24 hours inside a Wall Street investment bank at the beginning of the 2008 financial crisis. Late one night, a young analyst discovers that the firm’s financial model has broken down. If the market continues moving against them, their losses could become larger than the value of the company itself. The solution is simple, but brutal: sell everything before everyone else realizes what is happening.⁣
⁣
That decision becomes the moral center of the film. By unloading their toxic assets as quickly as possible, the firm might survive, but only by passing the damage on to clients and the rest of the market. Some of the characters understand exactly what this means. Others see it as nothing more than survival.⁣
⁣
What’s great is that 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥 (𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟏) manages to explain the basic problem of the 2008 crisis without drowning the audience in financial terminology. We understand enough to know that something has gone terribly wrong, while the focus remains on the people deciding what to do about it. Director J.C. Chandor made 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥 (𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟏) as his feature debut, and much of the movie takes place in offices and conference rooms. Yet it remains tense because the stakes are communicated almost entirely through conversations, silences and performances. This is subtle acting at its finest.⁣
⁣
Rate 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐥 (𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟏) out of ten. 👀

source_details.title: Margin Call
source_details.synopsis: Margin Call is a 2011 American drama film written and directed by J. C. Chandor in his directorial debut. The story takes place over 24 hours at a large Wall Street investment bank during the initial stages of the 2008 financial crisis. It focuses on the actions taken by a group of employees during the crisis. The title is a reference to a "margin call", the situation where a financial market participant must provide additional collateral for an existing financial market contract due to increased credit risk.
